title: Spec browser
summary: A `.spec` folder says what the code is meant to do. The app lets you read it.
description:
Code says what a program does, not what it was meant to do. A repository's `.spec` folder holds that: one JSON file per part of the product, all following one schema, next to the pictures they show.

The folders are the outline. An item's id is its path without `.spec/` and `.json`, and a folder's own item is its `index.json`.

requirements.text: Every `.json` file in `.spec` is one item. Every other file is an asset.
All items follow one schema, published as `schema/spec.schema.json`. The file is generated from the schema the app reads with, and a test fails when they differ.
A file that can't be read (not JSON, an unknown key, a missing title) is listed as a problem with the reason. The rest of the spec still shows.
A figure that isn't in the folder, a related id that leads nowhere and a requirement id used twice are listed as problems.
The whole folder loads in one request, so moving between items never waits.
The outline can be filtered by the words in titles, summaries, descriptions and requirements. A matching requirement opens its item with that requirement highlighted.
The spec of any branch can be browsed, and links inside it stay on that branch.
A path under an item's code opens that file or folder in the app.
A repository whose default branch has a spec shows a way into it on its overview.
Items can be nested three folders deep. A deeper folder is listed as a problem.

figures.alt: An item in the spec browser, with its requirements, a figure, code and related items
figures.caption: An item: status, requirements, pictures, and where it lives in the code.

questions: Should a pull request show which items its changed files belong to, from each item's `code`?
Should requirements name the tests that prove them?
Guests can't browse a spec: reading the folder in one request needs GitHub's GraphQL API, which needs a token. Worth a slower path over REST?
